 The 'Trump Bump' Gave Social Security a 3.6% Raise for 2027 - But There's a Catch
 Here's what you should know before celebrating higher benefits in 2027.
 By
 Paige Cerulli 
 ,
 Edited by
 Laura Hohenstein 
 Updated
 Nov. 9, 2026
 Fact checked 
 This article was subjected to a comprehensive fact-checking process. Our professional fact-checkers verify article information against primary sources, reputable publishers, and experts in the field.
 Add Us On Google
 Google Preferred Sources lets you customize your search results. By choosing to follow FinanceBuzz, you’re telling Google to prioritize content from a source you trust.
Americans receiving Social Security senior benefits 
may look forward to slightly larger monthly checks next year. On October 14, the 
Social Security Administration (SSA) announced a 3.6% 2027 cost-of-living 
adjustment (COLA), creating a boost in benefits. The COLA, designed to ensure 
benefits keep up with inflation, affects nearly 72 million beneficiaries 
receiving Social Security. It also increases payments for about 7.3 million 
people receiving Supplemental Security Income (SSI). 
Though the benefits increase may seem positive, there are a few catches that 
beneficiaries should be aware of. Here's what you should know about the COLA and 
other factors that might eat into the benefits increase before the money reaches 
your bank account.

 Did you know if your air conditioner stops working, your homeowner’s insurance won’t cover it? Same with plumbing, electrical issues, appliances, and more.

 The facts on the 2027 COLA
The 3.6% 2027 COLA is the largest since 2023. It increases benefits for retired 
workers by an average of $75, bringing benefits from about $2,095 to $2,170 per 
month. 
The COLA calculation is based on the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Consumer Price 
Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W) data. The calculation 
compares CPI-W data from the third quarter of the current year to data from the 
third quarter of the previous year. 
Social Security beneficiaries should see the COLA adjustment in January 2027. 
 SSI recipients should see the increase beginning on December 31, 2026. 
 Shopping for cheaper auto insurance? Enter your zip code here to get started. 
 The inflation behind the COLA
The COLA has been called the "Trump bump" in the media, a commentator's framing 
that references the inflation that drove the increase in benefits. That's the 
first catch. Though beneficiaries may look forward to receiving a benefits boost 
in 2027, the increase is due to the fact that inflation has climbed in 2026, and 
beneficiaries have been paying higher prices throughout the year already, long 
before receiving the increase. 
The large COLA means that prices rose, not that benefits gained ground. If 
inflation climbs steeply in the fourth quarter of 2026 and stays elevated 
throughout 2027, retirees may have to continue paying those higher prices for 
over a year without receiving more benefits to make up for those costs. That lag 
could take a financial toll, especially on retirees living on fixed incomes. 
 Medicare expenses
Medicare expenses may also quickly eat into any benefits increase. Medicare Part 
B premiums, which are deducted from Social Security checks, are predicted to 
increase in 2027. The 2026 Medicare Trustees Report projected that the Medicare 
Part B premium may increase from $202.90 in 2026 to $209.50 per month in 2027. 
CMS should announce the official Part B premiums later this year. 
Additionally, stand-alone Medicare Part D plans, which are a drug-only coverage 
paired with Original Medicare, may also see premium increases because of the end 
of a federal subsidy. CMS is ending the Part D Premium Stabilization Demonstration, 
which was designed to regulate climbing prices, at the end of 2026. Though the 
national average stand-alone premium is projected to rise less than $1 per month 
in 2027, individual plans could experience larger increases. 
According to KFF, Medicare Part B and D premiums and cost sharing account for 
nearly one quarter of a retiree's average monthly Social Security benefits. The 
additional expense of these higher premiums could quickly eat into retirees' 
extra Social Security benefits.

 How the COLA affects different beneficiaries' checks
The COLA is percentage-based, meaning the exact benefits increase depends on the 
size of a retiree's 2026 check. Higher earners who receive larger checks stand 
to see the largest increase in their benefits. Lower earners with smaller checks 
should receive a smaller increase in their benefits. 
 Does the COLA come up short
Groups like the Senior Citizens League have criticized the use of the CPI-W to 
 calculate the COLA . The CPI-W is based on the spending habits of working people, 
and those people tend to spend less on healthcare than retirees. According to 
the National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare, people 65 and 
older spend twice as much as younger Americans on out-of-pocket health and 
medical expenses. Additionally, Americans 75 and older spend nearly three times 
as much on those healthcare expenses, meaning the CPI-W may significantly 
under-reflect retirees' actual spending. 
Using different data to calculate the COLA might result in a figure that better 
reflects retirees' expenses. The Consumer Price Index for Americans 62 and 
Older, the CPI-E, is one alternative, but it's an experimental index that has 
sometimes increased less than the CPI-W. 
 Bottom line
To see how the COLA impacts your Social Security benefits, you may log into your 
my Social Security account to view your COLA notice starting in late November. 
You'll need to enroll in paperless notices to see your COLA notice online, and 
the notice includes the exact dates and dollar amounts of your new benefit. If 
you don't wish to create a my Social Security account or enroll in paperless 
benefits, you may receive your COLA notice by mail in December, about three 
weeks after it's available online. 
Once you know your benefit amount for 2027, it's a good idea to review your retirement plan and your 
monthly budget to make any needed changes.
